target_customer: Parents of children with smartphones who want to know where their kids are
problem: Parents want to know when children arrive at or leave places such as school or practice, without draining the phone battery or relying on coarse cell tower data.
business_model: Consumer app, monetization not stated in sources found
product_category: Family location tracking and geofencing smartphone app

founders.name: Mick Johnson
founders.background_notes: The YC page lists him as Founder/CEO and gives no background. Prior employers and education not found in sources opened.

founders.name: James Gregory
founders.background_notes: The YC page lists him as Founder/CTO and gives no background. Technical status inferred from the CTO title only, so left null.

competitors.name: AT&T FamilyMap
competitors.traction_then: Not stated; TechCrunch called it the main competitor

competitors.name: Google Latitude
competitors.what: General location sharing service, not built for parents

technical_complexity.rationale: Adaptive location sampling to balance accuracy and battery life, plus geofencing on early iOS 4 background location APIs, was real mobile engineering for a two person team.

defensibility.rationale: No network effects or data lock-in were described, and carriers and Google already offered similar location sharing, so copying was easy.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: AT&T FamilyMap and Google Latitude already covered the wedge in 2010. Whereoscope was later marked acquired by YC, but the acquirer is not public in sources found.

market_need_then: TechCrunch described the launch in August 2010 as part of a wave of location apps enabled by iOS 4, and as a possibly easier alternative to existing kid tracking options. A Xconomy profile noted the founders had to confront who actually needed such tracking. No spend or usage figures found.

branding.domain_note: Used whereoscope.com; no purchase history found.

brand_strength.rationale: Little press about the brand itself beyond a TechCrunch launch post and a Xconomy profile; a long invented name that suggests a scope for where.

outcome_analysis: Whereoscope launched in August 2010 as a geofencing family locator and was listed by YC as acquired, but the acquirer, date and terms are not public in sources found. The company's archived site says it closed on 2013-07-01, so the product ended about three years after launch. Direct competition from AT&T FamilyMap and Google Latitude and low defensibility suggest a small team outcome, but the cause is not documented.
notes: One aggregator reports about $120K from a single seed round with YC as investor; this is a single aggregator figure and is unverified, so not recorded as a round. The directory marks the company acquired while the archived site notice says it closed on 2013-07-01; the acquirer was not found. A separate current product named Whereoscope appears on a directory page and may be unrelated. The Xconomy article could not be fetched (503), only seen as a search snippet. Completeness pass: Seed of about $120K rests on a single aggregator (The Company Check, dated 2010-08-24); Seedtable dates a last round 2010-08-05 with no amount. The amount is above the standard YC deal reported by Xconomy for that batch, so it is unverified. Xconomy profile dated 2010-09-20 was not readable for funding text.
